title: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
summary: Why models break past their trained length, how PI, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN rescale RoPE per frequency, how Ring Attention and context parallelism fit million-token attention, and how to test real use.
outcomes: Explain why RoPE pairs whose wavelength exceeds the trained length break when the context is extended
Compute PI, NTK-aware and YaRN frequency scales and the YaRN attention factor for a given model and scale factor
Explain how Ring Attention computes exact attention by rotating KV blocks and merging them with an online softmax
Compute the minimum block size c >= F/B that hides ring communication, and balance causal work across ranks
Evaluate long-context models with passkey, Lost in the Middle and RULER instead of perplexity alone

lessons.title: Why models break past their trained length

blocks.md:
A transformer is trained on sequences up to some length $L$, its **context window** (2,048 tokens for LLaMA, 4,096 for Llama 2, 8,192 for Llama 3). Feed it a longer prompt and quality usually collapses, even though nothing in the weights depends on sequence length. Two separate walls stand in the way:

1. **The position encoding wall.** The model has never seen the position signals that appear past $L$, so attention scores become out of distribution.
2. **The memory and compute wall.** Attention compares every token with every other, so cost grows with the square of the length, and even the KV cache outgrows one GPU.

This course takes them in order: lessons 1 to 3 fix the first wall by rescaling RoPE (Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN), lessons 4 and 5 break the second by spreading attention across GPUs (Ring Attention, context parallelism), and lesson 6 asks whether the model actually *uses* the longer context.

Recall from the attention course that a score is the dot product $q_m^\top k_n$ of a query at position $m$ and a key at position $n$. **RoPE** (rotary position embedding, Su et al.) injects position by *rotating* those vectors. The head dimension $|D|$ is split into $|D|/2$ pairs, and pair $d$ is rotated by the angle $m\theta_d$, where

blocks.caption: The base b is 10000 in RoFormer and Llama 2 (Llama 3 raises it to 500,000). The wavelength lambda_d is how many tokens pair d needs to complete one full turn (notation from the YaRN paper).

blocks.md:
Because a rotation by $m\theta$ dotted with a rotation by $n\theta$ only depends on $(m-n)\theta$, the score depends on the *relative* distance. Low $d$ pairs spin fast (short wavelength) and resolve nearby order; high $d$ pairs spin slowly and act like a coarse clock over the whole window.

Take a toy head with $|D| = 8$ (4 pairs), $b = 10000$, trained on $L = 2048$. Then $\theta = 1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001$ radians per token and the wavelengths are 6.3, 62.8, 628.3 and 6,283.2 tokens.

blocks.title: Toy RoPE: which angles did training ever show?

scenes.caption: Wavelength and r = L / lambda, the number of full turns each pair makes across the 2,048 training positions. Pairs 0 to 2 wrap around many times; pair 3 completes only a third of a turn.
Angle (radians) at position 2047, the last trained position. Pair 3 has only ever seen angles between 0 and 2.047 rad.

At position 4095 pair 3 sits at 4.095 rad, an angle it never saw. Pairs 0 to 2 wrapped during training, so every angle on their circle is familiar. The fast pairs are fine; the slow pair is out of distribution.

blocks.md: Columns: wavelength $\lambda$, rotations $r = L/\lambda$, angle at position 2047, angle at position 4095. The same split happens in real models. For Llama 2 ($|D| = 128$, $b = 10000$, $L = 4096$), pairs 0 to 45 complete at least one turn within 4,096 tokens, but the 18 pairs $d = 46$ to $63$ have $\lambda > 4096$ (pair 63: about 54,410 tokens). Those slow pairs effectively encode *absolute* position, and past $L$ they produce angles the network has never seen.

blocks.title: RoPE wavelength per pair versus the trained length

scenes.caption: Llama 2 setting: base 10000, L = 4096. Every pair whose wavelength curve lies above the flat line never finishes a turn during training (pairs 46 to 63).
Llama 3 setting: base 500,000, L = 8192. A larger base stretches all wavelengths, so more pairs are slow; the crossing moves to a lower pair index.

blocks.prompt: LLaMA was pretrained at 2,048 tokens. If you simply fine-tune it on 8,192-token sequences without touching RoPE, how fast do you expect the usable context to grow?
blocks.reveal: Very slowly. The Position Interpolation paper fine-tuned LLaMA directly on longer sequences and after more than 10,000 batches the effective context window only moved from 2,048 to 2,560 tokens. The slow pairs must learn brand new angles, and the attention scores they produce can be wildly large out of distribution. That is why every method in the next two lessons changes the rotation itself instead.

blocks.md: RoPE is called a relative encoding, so it is tempting to think it should extrapolate for free. It does not: dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length never wrap, so in practice they leak absolute position, and new positions mean new, unseen angles.

Each RoPE pair has a wavelength $\lambda_d = 2\pi b^{2d/|D|}$. Pairs with $\lambda_d \ll L$ are safe at any length; pairs with $\lambda_d > L$ are the ones that break when you go past the trained window.

blocks.question: In the toy head (wavelengths 6.3, 62.8, 628.3, 6,283 tokens; trained on 2,048), which pair sees an out-of-distribution angle first as the prompt grows past 2,048 tokens?
options: Pair 0, because it rotates fastest and accumulates the largest angle
Pair 3, because it never completed a full turn during training
All pairs equally, because every position past 2,048 is new
None, because RoPE only depends on relative distance
blocks.explain: Pair 0 reaches huge raw angles but wraps every 6.3 tokens, so every angle on its circle was seen thousands of times. Pair 3 only ever covered 0 to 2.047 rad, so at position 2,100 it is already at 2.1 rad, outside its training range.

blocks.question: Raising the RoPE base b (as Llama 3 does with 500,000) changes the wavelengths how?
options: Every wavelength except pair 0's gets longer, so more pairs act as slow, absolute-position pairs
All wavelengths get shorter, so every pair wraps within the window
Only pair 0 changes
Wavelengths are fixed by the head dimension, not by b
blocks.explain: lambda_d = 2 pi b^(2d/|D|) grows with b for every d above 0 (pair 0 always has wavelength 2 pi). A bigger base spreads frequencies over a longer range, which is why it is used together with long-context training.

blocks.md: **Position Interpolation (PI)**, from Chen et al. at Meta (2023), makes one change: instead of feeding position $m$, feed $m/s$, where $s = L'/L$ is the **scale factor** from the trained length $L$ to the target $L'$. Every position in the long sequence is squeezed back into the trained range $[0, L)$, so no pair ever sees a new angle. Positions become fractional, which RoPE handles fine because angles are continuous.

blocks.caption: PI rescales the position index. Equivalently every frequency theta_d is divided by s.

blocks.md:
The paper proves the interpolated attention score has an upper bound at least about 600 times smaller than the extrapolated one in the LLaMA 7B setting, and shows that LLaMA 7B to 65B can be extended to 32,768 tokens with at most 1,000 fine-tuning steps.

The cost is precision. Interpolation shrinks *every* pair by $s$, including the fast ones that tell neighbouring tokens apart. In the toy head with $s = 4$, pair 0 now turns 0.25 rad per token instead of 1 rad, so adjacent tokens look four times closer than anything the model was trained on. The YaRN paper reports PI fine-tunes only reached roughly $s = 8$ before outputs degraded.

blocks.title: How much each method slows each RoPE pair (toy head, s = 4)

scenes.caption: Original RoPE: every pair keeps its trained frequency (factor 1). At position 4095 pair 3 hits 4.095 rad, outside the 0 to 2.047 rad it saw in training.
PI divides every frequency by s = 4. Pair 3 at position 4095 is now at 1.024 rad (seen), but pair 0 also slows to 0.25 rad per token: nearby tokens get blurred.
NTK-aware raises the base to b' = 10000 x 4^(8/6), about 63,496. The fastest pair keeps factor 1, the slowest gets exactly 1/s, and the middle pairs fall in between (0.63, 0.397).

blocks.md: **NTK-aware interpolation** (posted by bloc97 in 2023, written up in the YaRN paper, Appendix A.2) spreads the "interpolation pressure" unevenly: scale high frequencies less and low frequencies more. The simplest way is to change the base so that the *last* pair is slowed by exactly $s$ while pair 0 is untouched:

blocks.caption: Derived from requiring b'^((|D|-2)/|D|) = s b^((|D|-2)/|D|): the last pair, d = |D|/2 - 1, matches PI exactly.

blocks.md: For Llama 2 ($|D| = 128$) and $s = 16$, $b' \approx 167{,}199$. The per-pair slowdown then rises smoothly from 1.0 at pair 0 to 2.0 at pair 16, 4.1 at pair 32, 8.3 at pair 48 and 16 at pair 63. Code Llama applied the same base-change idea, raising the base from 10,000 to 1,000,000 for long-context fine-tuning. The name adjusted base frequency (ABF) comes from Xiong et al., Effective Long-Context Scaling of Foundation Models.

blocks.title: Per-pair frequency multiplier: PI vs NTK-aware (Llama 2)

scenes.caption: PI multiplies every pair by 1/s. NTK-aware keeps the fast pairs near 1 and only reaches 1/s at the slowest pair.
At s = 16 the gap is huge: PI slows even pair 0 sixteenfold, NTK-aware leaves pairs 0 to 10 within a factor 1.6 of the original.

Notice where NTK-aware still exceeds 1/s: pairs 46 to 62 have wavelengths above L, yet they are slowed by less than s, so at the target length they rotate past angles never seen in training (a mild extrapolation).

blocks.md: NTK-aware works much better than PI *without* fine-tuning, but the YaRN authors list two problems. Some pairs are slightly extrapolated to out-of-bound angles, so fine-tuning with it gave worse results than PI, and the nominal $s$ does not match the real extension, so in practice $s$ must be set higher than the target and the best base has to be found empirically.

Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.
Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

blocks.question: A Llama 2 model (L = 4096) is extended with PI to 16,384 tokens. What position value does RoPE receive for the token at index 10,000?
options: 4,096, clipped to the trained maximum
blocks.explain: s = 16384 / 4096 = 4, and PI feeds m / s = 10000 / 4 = 2500. Positions are scaled, not clipped; fractional values are allowed.

blocks.question: Why does PI hurt the fast (low d) RoPE pairs?
options: They overflow numerically at large positions
They are dropped entirely
Their wavelength becomes longer than the context, so they stop encoding anything
Dividing their frequency by s makes neighbouring tokens differ by a much smaller angle than in training, so local order is harder to resolve
blocks.explain: Pair 0 normally turns 1 rad per token; after PI with s = 4 it turns 0.25 rad. Nearby tokens become nearly indistinguishable in that pair, the high-frequency information the network relied on.

lessons.title: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature

blocks.md:
YaRN (Peng, Quesnelle, Fan, Shippole, 2023) makes the per-pair treatment explicit. It measures each pair by $r(d) = L/\lambda_d$, the number of full turns the pair makes during training, and applies a three-way rule that the paper calls **NTK-by-parts**:

- $r(d) > \beta$: many turns, the pair only encodes relative position. **Do not touch it.**
- $r(d) < \alpha$: less than one turn, the pair encodes absolute position. **Interpolate it fully, like PI** (never extrapolate).
- in between: blend linearly.

For the LLaMA family the paper found $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = 32$ work well. Positions are left as they are ($g(m) = m$); only the frequencies change.

blocks.caption: YaRN Eq. 11 and 13. gamma = 1 keeps the original frequency, gamma = 0 divides it by s.

blocks.title: YaRN on the toy head (L = 2048, s = 4)
blocks.code:
import math
b, D, L, s = 10000, 8, 2048, 4   # toy: 4 rotary pairs
alpha, beta = 1, 32              # ramp bounds (paper's Llama values)
for d in range(D // 2):
    theta = b ** (-2 * d / D)
    lam = 2 * math.pi / theta    # wavelength in tokens
    r = L / lam                  # rotations seen in training
    g = min(max((r - alpha) / (beta - alpha), 0), 1)
    scale = (1 - g) / s + g      # 1 = keep, 1/s = interpolate
    print(d, round(lam, 1), round(r, 2), round(g, 3), round(scale, 4))
mscale = 0.1 * math.log(s) + 1   # multiplies cos and sin
print("mscale", round(mscale, 4), "logits x", round(mscale ** 2, 4))

scenes.caption: Setup: 4 rotary pairs, trained length 2048, target 8192 (s = 4), ramp bounds alpha = 1 and beta = 32.
Pair 0: wavelength 6.3 tokens, 325.95 turns during training. r > beta, so gamma = 1 and the frequency is kept.
Pair 1: 32.59 turns, just above beta = 32, so it is also kept intact.
Pair 2: 3.26 turns sits inside the ramp. gamma = (3.26 - 1) / 31 = 0.073, so the scale is 0.927 / 4 + 0.073 = 0.3047, mostly interpolated.
Pair 3: a third of a turn, r < alpha, so gamma = 0 and it is fully interpolated (1/s = 0.25), exactly like PI.
Finally the attention temperature: cos and sin are multiplied by 0.1 ln 4 + 1 = 1.1386, which multiplies every logit by 1.2965.

blocks.md: At real scale, Llama 2 extended with $s = 16$ ($L = 4096$): pairs 0 to 20 have $r > 32$ and are untouched, pairs 46 to 63 have $r < 1$ and are divided by 16, and pairs 21 to 45 blend (pair 32, for example, has $r = 6.52$, $\gamma = 0.178$, and keeps 0.229 of its frequency). Hugging Face computes the same boundaries in closed form as fractional pair indices 20.94 and 45.03, which it floors and ceils to 20 and 46. Between them HF ramps linearly in pair index, not in $r$, so middle pairs differ from the paper's rule (pair 32 keeps about 0.567 of its frequency in HF, not 0.229).

blocks.title: YaRN ramp: frequency multiplier per pair (Llama 2, head dim 128)

scenes.caption: s = 16, alpha = 1, beta = 32: a flat 1 for the fast pairs, a flat 1/16 for the slow pairs, and a ramp between them. Compare the PI line at 1/s.
Add NTK-aware: it slows fast pairs a little (pair 16 by 2x) and under-slows pairs near the boundary. YaRN instead never touches pairs with more than 32 turns and never extrapolates the slow ones.
Narrow the ramp (beta = 8): more pairs keep their frequency. The boundaries are tuned per model family; the paper's Llama values are 1 and 32.

blocks.md: The second ingredient is a **temperature** $t$ on the attention logits. The authors observed that dividing logits by a suitable $t$ lowers perplexity uniformly across samples and positions of the extended window, and fitted the best value on LLaMA 7B to 65B:

blocks.caption: YaRN Eq. 14 and 15. For s = 8 this gives 1.208; for s = 16, 1.2773, so logits are multiplied by 1/t = 1.6314.

blocks.md: No attention code changes: since both $q$ and $k$ are rotated by the RoPE tables, multiplying cos and sin by $\sqrt{1/t}$ scales the logit by $1/t$. In Hugging Face transformers this is the `attention_factor` that the YaRN rope function returns alongside the new frequencies (default `0.1 * log(factor) + 1`). The factor is above 1, so it *sharpens* attention, offsetting the flatter distribution you get when a query is spread over many more keys.

blocks.title: YaRN attention factor versus scale factor

scenes.caption: The multiplier on cos and sin grows slowly with s: 1.069 at s = 2, 1.208 at s = 8, 1.347 at s = 32.
The logit multiplier is its square: 1.143, 1.459 and 1.813 at the same scales. The effect is real but gentle, logarithmic in s.

blocks.title: LLaMA 7B Proof-pile perplexity (YaRN Table 5, lower is better)

scenes.caption: No fine-tuning, s = 2, evaluated at 4,096 tokens. NTK-aware is worst here (5.97); YaRN 3.67 is best, just ahead of NTK-by-parts (3.71).
Fine-tuned 400 steps with s = 16, evaluated at 32,768 tokens: NTK-aware degrades to 8.49 while YaRN reaches 2.77, slightly ahead of NTK-by-parts (2.81) thanks to the temperature.

blocks.md: The paper fine-tuned Llama 2 7B and 13B with $s = 16$ for 400 steps (batch 64, 64K-token PG19 chunks), then $s = 32$ for 200 more, reaching 128K. It reports needing about 10x fewer tokens and 2.5x fewer training steps than previous methods. **Dynamic scaling** is an inference-only variant: recompute $s = \max(1, l'/L)$ from the current length $l'$ on every forward pass, so short prompts run unscaled.

With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

**Llama 3.1** ships its own by-parts rule. Meta's reference `apply_scaling` uses factor 8, low_freq_factor 1, high_freq_factor 4 and an original length of 8,192 with base 500,000 (comment: "Values obtained from grid search"). Pairs with wavelength under 8192/4 = 2,048 tokens are kept, those over 8,192 are divided by 8, and those between are smoothed. With head dim 128 that is 29 kept pairs, 6 smoothed and 29 divided. Unlike YaRN there is no attention factor (Hugging Face returns 1.0 for `rope_type: llama3`).

blocks.code:
# Hugging Face config fields (rope_scaling, called rope_parameters in newer versions)
# Llama 3.1 style: by-parts on wavelength thresholds, no temperature
{"rope_type": "llama3", "rope_theta": 500000.0, "factor": 8.0,
 "low_freq_factor": 1.0, "high_freq_factor": 4.0,
 "original_max_position_embeddings": 8192}

# YaRN: required keys; beta_fast / beta_slow default to 32 / 1
{"rope_type": "yarn", "factor": 4.0,
 "original_max_position_embeddings": 32768}
blocks.caption: Key names follow the validators in transformers' modeling_rope_utils.py. The YaRN example values are illustrative, not from a specific model card.

blocks.md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

blocks.question: Under YaRN with alpha = 1 and beta = 32, a RoPE pair completes 50 full turns within the original training length. What happens to its frequency when you extend by s = 8?
options: It is unchanged
It is divided by 8
It is divided by about 4, halfway along the ramp
It is multiplied by 8 to compensate
blocks.explain: r = 50 > beta = 32, so gamma = 1 and h(theta) = theta. High-frequency pairs only carry relative position, which is already in distribution at any length.

blocks.question: A colleague implements YaRN by scaling queries by 1.2773 for s = 16 but forgets the keys. What is the effect on the logits?
options: Correct: the temperature is defined on queries only
Logits are unchanged because softmax is scale invariant
Logits are scaled by 1.2773 instead of the intended 1.6314
Logits are scaled by 1.6314 squared
blocks.explain: YaRN multiplies both rotated q and k (via cos and sin) by sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln 16 + 1 = 1.2773, so the dot product is scaled by 1.2773 squared = 1.6314. Scaling only one side gives just 1.2773. Softmax is shift invariant, not scale invariant.

blocks.question: For Llama 3.1 (base 500,000, original length 8,192, factor 8, high_freq_factor 4), a pair has wavelength 1,500 tokens. How is it scaled?
options: Divided by 8
Smoothed between 1 and 1/8
Kept unchanged
Divided by 4
blocks.explain: High-frequency threshold = 8192 / 4 = 2048 tokens. A wavelength of 1,500 is below it, so the frequency is kept. Only wavelengths above 8,192 are divided by 8, with smoothing in between.

blocks.md: Fixing RoPE lets the model *understand* position 100,000. It does not make position 100,000 *fit*. Take Llama 3 8B: 32 layers, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention) of dimension 128, stored in bf16 (2 bytes). The KV cache costs

blocks.caption: So 1 GiB at 8K tokens, 16 GiB at 128K and 128 GiB at 1M tokens, before weights or activations.

blocks.md: A naive attention that materializes the score matrix is far worse: one head at 128K tokens needs $131072^2 \times 2$ bytes = 32 GiB in bf16, *per head, per layer*. Memory-efficient (blockwise) attention, the FlashAttention idea, never stores that matrix; it streams key and value blocks and keeps a running softmax. But even then, the Ring Attention paper points out that each layer's *output* for the whole sequence must still be stored on one device, and accelerators have less than 100 GB of HBM.

blocks.title: Memory at long context (Llama 3 8B shapes, bf16)

scenes.caption: The KV cache grows linearly: 16 GiB at 128K tokens with 8 KV heads. Slide KV heads to 32 to see why grouped-query attention matters (64 GiB).
A materialized score matrix grows quadratically: 32 GiB for a single head at 128K and 2 TiB at 1M. This is the term blockwise attention eliminates.

blocks.md: Blockwise attention works because softmax can be computed **incrementally**. Keep three numbers per query: the running maximum score $m$, the running denominator $\ell = \sum e^{s_i - m}$ and the running unnormalized output $o = \sum e^{s_i - m} v_i$. When a new block arrives with a larger maximum, rescale the old $\ell$ and $o$ by $e^{m_{old} - m_{new}}$. The final answer is $o/\ell$, identical to the full softmax. Crucially, blocks can be merged in **any order**.

blocks.title: Merging two KV blocks with an online softmax
blocks.code:
import math
def merge(state, scores, values):
    m, l, o = state
    m_new = max(m, max(scores))
    c = math.exp(m - m_new)      # rescale old sums
    l = l * c + sum(math.exp(x - m_new) for x in scores)
    o = o * c + sum(math.exp(x - m_new) * v for x, v in zip(scores, values))
    return m_new, l, o

state = (-math.inf, 0.0, 0.0)
state = merge(state, [2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0])  # local KV block
state = merge(state, [3.0, 0.5], [3.0, 4.0])  # block from neighbor
m, l, o = state
print(round(o / l, 4))

scenes.caption: Start empty: m = minus infinity, l = 0, o = 0. One query will see 4 keys split into two blocks of 2.
Local block: scores 2.0 and 1.0, values 1 and 2. m = 2, l = 1 + e^-1 = 1.3679, o = 1 + 2e^-1 = 1.7358. Partial answer o / l = 1.2689.
Block from the neighbour: scores 3.0 and 0.5. New max 3, so old sums are rescaled by e^(2-3) = 0.3679 before adding. l = 1.5853, o = 3.9669.
o / l = 2.5023, exactly the output of a full softmax over all 4 scores (weights 0.232, 0.085, 0.631, 0.052). No 4-wide score row was ever stored.

blocks.md: **Ring Attention** (Liu, Zaharia, Abbeel, 2023) turns this order freedom into a distributed algorithm. Split the sequence into $N$ blocks and give host $i$ block $i$: its queries, keys and values. Arrange hosts in a ring. At each step every host computes blockwise attention of its *local queries* against the KV block it currently holds, and at the same time sends that KV block to the next host and receives one from the previous host. After $N$ steps every query block has met every KV block, and the result is **exact** attention.

blocks.title: Ring Attention with 4 hosts: KV blocks rotate, queries stay

scenes.caption: Step 1: host i attends its query block Qi to its own KV block KVi, while already sending KVi to host i+1 (dots on the arrows).
Step 2: each host now holds its predecessor's block. Host 0 attends Q0 to KV3, host 1 attends Q1 to KV0, and the next transfer is already in flight.
Step 3: blocks have travelled two hops. Only neighbour to neighbour links are used, so this maps onto GPU all-to-all fabrics and TPU torus links alike.
Step 4: last block, no further send. Every host has merged all 4 KV blocks into its online softmax, then runs the feedforward on its own block. Then the next layer starts.

blocks.prompt: Each host must hold its query block, the KV block it is computing on, a buffer for the KV block arriving, and its output. With block size c, batch b and hidden size h in bf16, how does per-host activation memory depend on the total sequence length?
blocks.reveal: It does not. The paper counts six blocks: 1 for queries, 2 for current K and V, 2 for the incoming K and V, 1 for the output, giving 6bch bytes per layer. Total sequence length only changes how many hosts (or steps) you need. That is why maximum context scales with device count: in their experiments 8 A100s gave 8x the previous best and TPUv4-1024 gave up to 512x.

blocks.md: Ring Attention is not an approximation like sparse or sliding-window attention. Each query still attends to every key; only the *order* and *location* of the work change. It also does not reduce FLOPs: total compute is the same quadratic amount, just spread over more chips.

Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

blocks.question: With Ring Attention on N hosts, after how many compute steps has host 0's query block seen every KV block of the sequence (one layer, forward pass)?
options: N
log2 N
N squared
blocks.explain: Each step delivers one new KV block from the predecessor. Host 0 starts with its own block and needs N - 1 more hops, so N compute steps in total (Algorithm 1 loops over the N - 1 transfers).

blocks.question: A KV block arrives whose maximum score (5.0) exceeds the running maximum (3.0). What must the online softmax do with its existing denominator l and output o?
options: Multiply both by e^(3 - 5) before adding the new terms
Discard them and restart from the new block
Multiply only o by e^(5 - 3)
Nothing; maxima only matter for the final normalization
blocks.explain: Old terms were exponentiated relative to max 3. To express them relative to the new max 5, multiply by e^(3-5) = e^-2. Then add the new block's terms computed with max 5. Skipping this gives wrong weights.

lessons.title: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses

blocks.md: Ring Attention is only free if sending a KV block takes no longer than computing on it. The paper's arithmetic, for block size $c$ (tokens), hidden size $d$ (not the RoPE pair index from earlier lessons), per-host compute $F$ (FLOP/s) and link bandwidth $B$ (bytes/s): blockwise attention costs $2dc^2$ FLOPs for $QK^\top$ plus $2dc^2$ for multiplying by $V$, and the K and V blocks are $2cd$ bytes each in bf16.

blocks.caption: Ring Attention Sec. 3. The hidden size cancels: the minimum block depends only on the hardware's FLOPs-to-bandwidth ratio.

blocks.md: Plug in an A100 (312 TFLOP/s bf16 peak, as in the paper's Table 2): over NVLink at 300 GB/s, $c \ge 1{,}040$ tokens; over InfiniBand at 12.5 GB/s, $c \ge 24{,}960$. The paper then asks for a per-host sequence of about $6c$ (6,240 and 149,760 tokens; the paper's Table 2 prints 6.2K and 149.5K). Worked example with $c = 4096$, $d = 4096$: compute takes $4 \cdot 4096^3 / 312\times10^{12} = 0.881$ ms, the 67.1 MB K plus V block takes 0.224 ms on NVLink but 5.37 ms on InfiniBand.

blocks.title: One host in a 4-host ring, c = 4096, d = 4096 (simplified)

scenes.caption: NVLink: each 0.224 ms transfer hides under a 0.881 ms compute step. Four steps finish at 3.52 ms, exactly the pure compute time.
InfiniBand at 12.5 GB/s: each transfer takes 5.37 ms, so compute idles waiting for the next block. The same work ends at about 17 ms, almost 5x slower. Here c = 4096 is far below F/B = 24,960.

blocks.title: Compute versus transfer time per ring step

scenes.caption: A100 over NVLink: transfer grows linearly in c, compute quadratically. They cross at c = F/B = 1,040 tokens; beyond it the transfer is hidden.
Drop bandwidth to 12.5 GB/s (InfiniBand in the paper's table): the crossover moves to 24,960 tokens, so each host needs much longer blocks to stay compute bound.

blocks.md: **Causal masking breaks the balance.** In a decoder, query block $i$ only needs KV blocks $0..i$. With contiguous blocks, host 0 has almost nothing to do while the last host does a full row of work, yet the ring advances in lockstep. **Striped Attention** (Brandon et al., 2023) fixes this by giving each device tokens spread uniformly through the sequence, reporting up to 1.45x end-to-end speedup at 256K on A100s and TPUv4s. Llama 3 uses a related trick: split the sequence into $2 \times CP$ chunks and give rank $i$ chunks $i$ and $2 \times CP - 1 - i$.

blocks.title: Causal attention work by rank (8 chunks, 4 ranks): value = owning rank

scenes.caption: Contiguous split: rank 0 owns query chunks 0 and 1, rank 3 owns 6 and 7. Masked (upper) cells are skipped. Rank 3's rows are the longest.
Llama 3 style zigzag: rank i owns chunks i and 7 - i. Each rank now gets one short row and one long row.

blocks.title: Causal work per rank, in chunk-pairs (diagonal counts as half)

scenes.caption: Contiguous: 2, 6, 10, 14. The step time is set by the busiest rank, so ranks 0 to 2 idle most of the time.
Zigzag (chunks i and 7 - i): 8, 8, 8, 8. Same total of 32, perfectly balanced.

blocks.md: Llama 3 also did **not** use a ring: its context parallelism first **all-gathers** K and V, then computes attention for the local query chunk. The paper accepts the exposed communication because all-gather makes masks such as document masks easy, and with grouped-query attention K and V are much smaller than Q, while attention compute is $O(S^2)$ against $O(S)$ for the gather.

**DeepSpeed Ulysses** (Jacobs et al., 2023) takes a different route. Each GPU holds a sequence shard; before attention an **all-to-all** reshuffles Q, K and V so each GPU holds the *full sequence* for a subset of heads, runs ordinary attention, and a second all-to-all returns to sequence sharding. Per-link volume is $4Nh/P$ (aggregate $3Nh$ for QKV plus $Nh$ for the output), constant when sequence length $N$ and GPUs $P$ grow together.

blocks.title: Ulysses all-to-all on 4 GPUs (T = token chunk, H = head)

scenes.caption: Before attention: GPU g holds token chunk g for all 4 heads (sequence parallel layout).
After the all-to-all: GPU g holds head g for all 4 token chunks, so it can run exact attention for that head locally. A second all-to-all reverses this after attention.

blocks.md: Choosing a scheme: Ulysses splits by heads, so (following from its layout) its parallel degree cannot exceed the number of heads, and every GPU still holds the full sequence for its heads. Ring Attention has no head limit and keeps per-device memory proportional to the block, but needs blocks above F/B and load balancing for causal masks. All-gather CP (Llama 3) is simplest and handles arbitrary masks, at the cost of exposed communication.

Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, TPU ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

blocks.question: You move a Ring Attention job from NVLink (300 GB/s) to a 25 GB/s network with the same GPUs (312 TFLOP/s). Roughly what minimum block size now hides communication?
options: 1,040 tokens, unchanged since hidden size cancels
About 87 tokens
About 12,480 tokens
It can never be hidden on a slower link
blocks.explain: c >= F / B = 312e12 / 25e9 = 12,480. Bandwidth dropped 12x, so the minimum block grows 12x. The hidden size cancels, but the bandwidth does not.

blocks.question: Ring Attention with 4 ranks and contiguous chunks shows rank 3 at full utilization and rank 0 mostly idle on a causal model. Which change fixes this without changing the math?
options: Increase the block size c
Assign each rank tokens or chunks spread across the sequence (striped or zigzag)
Switch to bidirectional attention
Reduce the number of KV heads
blocks.explain: The imbalance comes from the causal triangle: later query chunks attend to more keys. Striped Attention or Llama 3's chunk i plus chunk 2CP - 1 - i assignment gives every rank the same amount of unmasked work.

blocks.question: Why does DeepSpeed Ulysses' per-link communication stay constant as you scale sequence length and GPU count together?
options: It compresses activations to 1 bit
It only communicates the KV cache once per training run
It never communicates; each GPU attends locally
An all-to-all over P GPUs moves M/P per link, and the message M = 4Nh grows with N at the same rate as P
blocks.explain: Per-link volume is 4Nh/P. Doubling both N and P leaves it unchanged. With h = 4096 and N = 32K tokens per GPU, that is about 1.07 GB per layer in bf16 at P = 2, 4, 8 or 16.

lessons.title: Does the model use its context? Evaluation

blocks.md: A model that *accepts* 128K tokens is not necessarily a model that *uses* them. Perplexity, the usual long-context metric in extension papers (YaRN reports sliding-window perplexity on Proof-pile and GovReport), mostly rewards predicting the next token from nearby text. It can keep improving while retrieval from far away silently fails. So long-context work is evaluated with tasks where the answer can only come from a specific distant spot.

- **Passkey retrieval** (used by PI and YaRN): hide a five-digit number in filler text and ask for it. YaRN reports its 128K Llama 2 model passes with very high accuracy across the whole window.
- **Needle in a haystack**: the same idea with a sentence planted at varying depths and lengths. Llama 3 reports 100% retrieval at all depths and lengths, and also a multi-needle variant (4 needles, retrieve 2).
- **Position-controlled QA**: Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., 2023) moves the document containing the answer through 10, 20 or 30 retrieved documents.

blocks.title: GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy by answer position, 20 docs

scenes.caption: Answer document first: 75.8%. Answer last: 63.2%. This is the U-shape: primacy and recency are strong (Lost in the Middle, Table 6).
Answer in the middle (position 10): 53.8%, below the 56.1% the model scores with no documents at all (closed-book). Adding the right document in the wrong place made it worse than adding nothing.

blocks.prompt: The 16K-context version of GPT-3.5-Turbo was also tested on the same 20-document prompts (about 3K tokens on average, which fit in both). Would you expect the 16K model to use the middle documents better?
blocks.reveal: No. The paper finds the extended-context model's curve nearly superimposed on the standard one (for example 54.1% vs 53.8% at position 10). A bigger window raises the ceiling on what fits, not how well the model uses what is inside it.

blocks.md: **RULER** (Hsieh et al., 2024) generalizes needle tests into 13 synthetic tasks in four categories: retrieval (with multiple keys, values and distractors), multi-hop tracing, aggregation, and question answering, at configurable lengths. It defines a model's **effective length** as the longest tested length whose average score stays above Llama 2 7B's score at 4K, 85.6%. Of 17 models claiming 32K or more, only about half held that threshold at 32K.

blocks.title: RULER average score by length (Table 3); threshold 85.6%

scenes.caption: Llama 3.1 8B, claimed 128K: drops below 85.6% after 32K (84.7% at 64K), so its effective length is 32K.
Mistral 7B v0.2, claimed 32K: 75.4% at 32K and 13.8% at 128K, effective length 16K. Both score near-perfectly on passkey and vanilla needle tests at their claimed lengths.
Gemini 1.5 Pro, claimed 1M: 94.4% even at 128K, effective length above 128K, the longest length tested. Some models do hold up; you have to measure.

blocks.md: Putting the pieces together, the Llama 3 report shows what a production recipe checks. Llama 3 405B grew its context in **six stages** from 8K to 128K using about **800B tokens** of long-context pretraining, and moved to the next stage only when (1) short-context evaluations had fully recovered and (2) the model perfectly solved needle-in-a-haystack up to the current length. It also masks attention between different documents packed into one sequence, which it found important for continued pretraining on very long sequences.

Do not trust a single number. Low perplexity, a passing passkey test and a large advertised window can all coexist with poor use of mid-context information. Test retrieval at many depths, multi-hop and aggregation tasks, and short-context regressions.

Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

blocks.question: A team extends a 4K model to 64K with YaRN. Perplexity on long documents improves steadily up to 64K, and a single-needle test passes at every depth. What is the most informative next evaluation?
options: Run harder tasks (multi-key retrieval, multi-hop tracing, aggregation) across lengths, plus short-context benchmarks for regressions
Nothing, both checks passed
Report perplexity at 128K too
Retrain from scratch at 64K to be sure
blocks.explain: RULER shows models that pass vanilla needle tests still drop sharply on harder tasks as length grows. Llama 3 also gated each stage on recovering short-context quality. Perplexity rewards local prediction and says little about distant retrieval.

blocks.question: In Lost in the Middle (20 documents, GPT-3.5-Turbo), where should a RAG system place the most relevant retrieved passage?
options: In the middle, so the model reads context on both sides
At the very beginning (or end) of the context
It does not matter for models with a 16K window
Randomly, to avoid bias
blocks.explain: Accuracy was 75.8% with the answer first and 63.2% last, but 53.8% in the middle, below closed-book. The bigger 16K variant showed the same curve.
